issues: whether the use of unpublished screening criteria and a pre-classifying reference chart that assigns job titles to qualifying or non-qualifying categories constitutes an abuse of authority in a federal public service staffing process
whether the employer's interpretation of an open-ended qualification requirement (e.g. 'recent' experience, 'quasi-judicial' function) was reasonable in light of the posting language

whether the Public Service Staffing Tribunal applies a reasonableness standard or a correctness standard when reviewing the employer's interpretation of qualification requirements and the application of screening criteria
whether the Federal Court will defer to the PSST's acceptance of the employer's explanation on judicial review, or whether it will re-examine the reasonableness of the employer's interpretation

whether the staffing process was procedurally fair, including the right to be heard, the opportunity to provide further detail about duties, and the adequacy of an informal discussion before a final screening decision
whether inconsistent application of screening criteria to similarly situated candidates supports a finding of unfairness or abuse of authority

whether the employer's motive in shaping the criteria (e.g. protecting a group of officers whose positions were to be eliminated by pending legislative reform) is relevant to the abuse of authority analysis

whether the legal distinction between quasi-judicial and administrative functions is tenable where both roles exercise delegated decision-making authority under the same statute and perform substantially similar work
what remedies are available for a successful staffing complaint, including re-screening, appointment, or damages for loss of opportunity
key_facts: twelve years as a front-line immigration officer in the federal department administering immigration
internal competition for adjudicator position at the federal tribunal hearing protection claims
posting required 'recent' experience in decision-making or research in a judicial or quasi-judicial setting or in immigration, without specifying a time frame
employer internally fixed 'recent' at twelve months within the past five years, disclosed only after screening
employer provided screening committees a reference guide and a chart pre-classifying job titles as qualifying or non-qualifying
chart classified pre-removal risk assessment officers as making quasi-judicial decisions and front-line immigration officers as making purely administrative ones
only four months in the risk-assessment role was credited; twelve years of front-line work was not
client argues both roles are ministerial delegates under the same statute and perform essentially the same work
court decisions held risk-assessment officers are not a quasi-judicial body
union-management minutes suggest criteria were shaped to protect risk-assessment officers facing elimination by pending legislative reform
client requested informal discussion and offered further detail about duties; employer refused to reconsider
some other candidates were allowed to continue past screening
causes_of_action: abuse of authority in a federal public service staffing process
unfair or procedurally deficient screening process
search_terms: standard of review Federal Court PSST
